newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Congress passes securities reform bill.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Congress passes securities reform bill.

text.p: Congress on Tuesday passed a major securities bill that overhauls regulation of mutual funds and gives the Securities and Exchange Commission $20 million in additional funds to supervise investment advisers.
The Senate sent the bill to President Clinton on a voice vote after House approval on Saturday. Clinton is expected to sign it.

The bill exempts from state regulation securities offered by mutual funds and stocks listed on the New York Stock Exchange, American Stock Exchange, NASDAQ and other exchanges identified by the SEC as providing comparable listing standards.

It establishes an electronic database for disciplinary records of investment advisory funds and advisors that can be checked by individual investors through a toll-free telephone number. The bill calls for state regulation of the nation's 150,000 investment advisers while the SEC will oversee firms.

The bill, which is endorsed by the SEC, would also cut fees that public corporations pay for routine filings with the SEC by $850 million over 10 years and let brokerage firms borrow from other financial institutions besides banks.
Sponsors of the bill called it the first major overhaul of securities law in 50 years and said it would promote efficiency in capital markets.
"This bill represents a triumph of reason and moderation over extremism and ideology," Rep. Ed Markey, D-Massachusetts, said.

"The bill strikes a proper balance by eliminating overlapping state and federal regulation, yet without undermining investor protection," said Mark Griffin, president of the North American Securitiies Administrators Association.
Sen. Alfonse D'Amato, R-New York, chairman of the Banking Committee, said the bill created "a truly national mutual fund marketplace with uniform standards that will benefit investors and consumers."
